records.name: Health Signal
records.definition: A machine-readable signal that reports whether a component is currently healthy, or that a fault or anomaly in it has been detected.

records.name: Reduced Mean Time to Recovery
records.definition: The ability to shorten the mean time to recover from a failure by acting automatically.

records.name: Blind Routing
records.definition: Routing traffic to instances without checking their health, so requests hit dead or degraded nodes.

records.name: Observable Health Criteria
records.definition: The requirement that explicit, observable criteria define when a component counts as healthy.

records.name: Readiness/Liveness Routing
records.definition: The ability to route traffic only to instances that report themselves ready and alive.

records.name: Continuity During Failure
records.definition: The ability to keep serving requests by switching to a standby when the primary fails.

records.name: Health Detection
records.definition: The ability to detect that a component has failed so a switchover can be triggered.

records.name: Single Instance Dependency
records.definition: Depending on a single instance with no standby, so its failure takes down the whole service.

records.name: Replication or Alternate Capacity
records.definition: The requirement that duplicate copies or spare capacity exist to take over when a component fails.

records.name: Consistency Lag
records.definition: The degree to which replicas trail the primary, so reads served from them may return stale data.

records.name: Consistency Policy
records.definition: The requirement that a defined policy specify how and when replicas converge to a consistent state.

records.name: Read Scaling
records.definition: The ability to serve more read traffic by distributing it across replicas.

records.name: Single Copy State
records.definition: Keeping only one copy of state, so its loss or unavailability takes down the whole system.

records.name: Cost/Cold Start
records.definition: The degree to which scaling capacity up and down incurs added cost and cold-start latency.

records.name: Fixed Capacity
records.definition: Provisioning a fixed, preset amount of capacity, rather than adapting it to demand.

records.name: Horizontal Scalability
records.definition: The degree to which a system can grow by adding more interchangeable instances rather than enlarging one.

records.name: Incident Reduction

distinctFrom.reason: Incident reduction lowers how many incidents reach a responder, while reduced mean time to recovery shortens each one that happens.

records.definition: The ability to reduce the number of incidents that reach human responders by fixing them automatically.

records.name: Manual Remediation
records.definition: Recovering from incidents through human-operated fixes, rather than automated remediation.

records.name: Remediation Workflow
records.definition: A defined corrective action, or sequence of steps, carried out to return a system to a healthy state after a fault is detected.

records.name: Unsafe Automation
records.definition: The degree to which automated remediation may take wrong or harmful corrective actions, for example on a faulty signal, faster than the developer can intervene.

records.name: Data Migration Compatibility
records.definition: The degree to which reverting code is constrained by forward data migrations that cannot easily be undone.

records.name: Fast Failure Recovery
records.definition: The ability to recover quickly from a bad release by reverting to the last good version.

records.name: Irreversible Deployment

distinctFrom.reason: An irreversible deployment cannot roll back a release, while an irreversible migration cannot roll back a schema or data change.

records.definition: Deploying in a way that cannot be undone, so a bad release cannot be rolled back.

records.name: Reversible Deployment
records.definition: The requirement that a deployment be structured so it can be safely reverted to a prior version.

records.name: Versioned Artifact
records.definition: A build artifact tagged with a distinct version so a prior one can be redeployed.

records.name: In-Place Mutation Only
records.definition: Upgrading by mutating the running environment in place, with no parallel target to cut over to or fall back from.

records.name: Infrastructure Cost
records.definition: The degree to which running two full parallel environments doubles infrastructure cost during a cutover.

records.name: Low-Risk Cutover
records.definition: The ability to switch traffic to a new version with low risk by keeping the old one ready to fall back to.

records.name: Parallel Environments
records.definition: The requirement that two full production-equivalent environments run side by side for cutover.

records.name: Controlled Exposure
records.definition: The ability to expose a new version to a small, controlled fraction of traffic first.

records.name: Progressive Delivery
records.definition: A release strategy that rolls out changes gradually to widening audiences while monitoring for regressions.

records.name: Rollout Complexity
records.definition: The degree to which staging a release in gradual increments adds orchestration complexity.

records.name: Traffic Splitting
records.definition: A facility that routes a configurable proportion of traffic to different versions of a service.

records.name: Empirical Resilience Verification
records.definition: The ability to verify a system's resilience empirically by injecting faults and observing recovery.

records.name: Production Risk
records.definition: The degree to which deliberately injecting faults in production risks causing user-facing incidents.

records.name: Untested Failure Assumptions
records.definition: Assuming a system will survive failures without ever testing those assumptions against injected faults.

records.name: Connection Cleanup
records.definition: The ability to close open connections cleanly when a process shuts down.

records.name: Hard Process Kill
records.definition: Terminating a process abruptly without draining work, dropping in-flight requests and risking corrupt state.

records.name: In-Flight Work Drain

distinctFrom.reason: Draining finishes or hands off work in progress, while connection cleanup closes the open connections.

records.definition: The ability to finish or safely hand off in-progress work before a process exits.

records.name: Lifecycle Signals
records.definition: The requirement that a process receive lifecycle signals telling it when to start draining and stop.

records.name: Shutdown Latency
records.definition: The degree to which draining in-flight work before exit lengthens the time a shutdown takes.

records.name: Disk-Failure Survival

distinctFrom.reason: Disk-failure survival is continuing to serve data after a disk is lost, while parity-based recovery is one way the lost data is rebuilt.

records.definition: The ability to keep serving data after one or more disks fail, by reconstructing from redundancy.

records.name: Multiple Physical Disks
records.definition: The requirement that data span several physical disks so redundancy can survive a single-disk loss.

records.name: Parity-Based Recovery
records.definition: The ability to reconstruct lost data from parity information stored across the disk array.

records.name: Single-Disk Point of Failure
records.definition: Storing data on a single disk with no redundancy, so that one disk's failure loses everything.

records.name: Write Amplification
records.definition: The degree to which maintaining parity on writes multiplies the underlying disk writes for each logical write.

records.name: Recovery Policy
records.definition: A technique for declaring, per failure class, the action the system takes to restore service and who is told.

records.name: Expand-Contract Migration
records.definition: A technique for changing a schema in steps, adding the new shape, moving every reader and writer, then removing the old shape.

records.name: Dual Read and Write
records.definition: A technique for writing to both the old and the new store and comparing reads during a migration, until the new store is trusted.

records.name: Rollback Plan
records.definition: A technique for stating before a release how it is undone and testing that the undo works.

records.name: Small-Batch Release
records.definition: A technique for shipping changes in small increments, so each release has a small blast radius.

records.name: Backup
records.definition: A technique for copying data to separate storage on a schedule, so it can be restored after loss or corruption.

records.name: Automate the Runbook
records.definition: A technique for turning repeated manual operational steps into a script the system runs and logs.

records.name: Autoscaling Policy
records.definition: A technique for declaring the load signals and limits by which the number of instances grows and shrinks.
